newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr rise fuels Japan insurers' foreign bond demand.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rise fuels Japan insurers' foreign bond demand.

text.p: The dollar's rapid rise has made yield-hungry Japanese life insurers even more eager to pour their money into offshore bonds, fund managers said on Friday.

More investors are looking for higher returns by investing in foreign-currency based bonds, mainly U.S. Treasuries, in a growing consensus that interest rate differentials between the United States and Japan will not shrink dramatically, they said.

"Under the current situation, it is more likely that foreign bond holdings will expand in the next fiscal year (starting April) rather than shrink," said Koshi Watanabe, foreign bond investment manager at Chiyoda Mutual Life Insurance Co.

Watanabe said in his personal opinion the yen's downward trend may persist. Also, the pace of economic growth in Japan could stay sluggish over a protracted period, keeping Japanese interest rates low.

"There is a limit on the amount of fixed income you can raise by only investing in domestic interest rates, with the key overnight call rate staying below 0.5 percent and the key 10-year government bond staying around 2.4 percent," Watanabe said.
"If such a trend persists in Japan, it's natural that we have to buy foreign assets," he said.
Fund managers said they had grown more comfortable about investing in foreign bonds as the possibility of another sharp appreciation of the yen had receded.
"The dollar's bullish trend should continue due to healthy economic fundamentals," said Michihisa Tanimoto, foreign bond and forex section manager at Sumitomo Life Insurance Co.

Tanimoto said the dollar scaled new heights after the market grew sceptical about the chance of a coordinated foray by the U.S. and Japanese authorities in the currency markets to slow the ascent of the greenback.
"There has been no change in our strategy since the recent upward trend (in the dollar)," Tanimoto said. "We'll keep on gradually increasing foreign bond holdings in our portfolio."
Tanimoto forecast the dollar would move in a range of 117 to 122 yen between now and the end of March. However, he said he was not planning to buy the greenback aggressively around 120 yen.
"We'll keep our stance of buying-on-dips for now," he added.

The dollar surged to 120 yen in late Tokyo trade, spurred on by comments from Japanese policy makers saying that the weak yen poses no threat to the Japanese economy. It had stood at around 119 yen in late U.S. trading.
Dai-Ichi Life Insurance said it may exceed its original target of 100 billion yen ($833 million) in offshore portfolio investments in the period from October to March 31.

Nippon Dantai Life Insurance Co, which had led foreign bond buying by domestic insurers in the first half of the current fiscal year, has been taking profits by selling U.S. Treasuries on the dollar's rallies above 117 yen.
"We are in a phase of taking profits by selling cash Treasuries," said Masanori Mizoguchi, general manager of securities investment department at Nippon Dantai.
"We have already built up a large quantity of foreign bond holdings," Mizoguchi said. "But after profit-taking, we may look for chances to invest on major dips." ($1=120 yen)
